items.stem: What kind of mouth does Kamaswami have?
items.quote: with a greedy mouth
items.why: The merchant's face hints at his love of gain.

items.stem: How often does Siddhartha eat each day in the merchant's house?
items.quote: Siddhartha only ate once a day
items.why: He keeps a Samana's habit.

items.stem: What does Kamaswami hand Siddhartha to read?
items.quote: Kamaswami left the room and returned with a scroll
items.why: He tests whether his guest can read.

items.stem: What does Siddhartha refuse to drink in the merchant's house?
items.quote: ate neither meat nor did he drink wine
items.why: He keeps some of his old habits.

items.stem: A servant prepares a bath for Siddhartha every day.
items.quote: every day a servant prepared a bath for him
items.why: He now lives in comfort.

items.stem: Siddhartha comes home angry and tired from the rice trip.
items.quote: returned extremely satisfied from his trip
items.why: He returns very satisfied.

items.stem: Complete: “cheat him out of some small change when buying ____”
items.quote: cheat him out of some small change when buying bananas
items.why: He does not mind being cheated a little.

items.stem: Complete: “gave copper-coins to their ____”
items.quote: gave copper-coins to their children
items.why: He spends his time kindly in the village.

items.stem: Match each person to what Siddhartha says he gives.
items.why: Everyone gives what he has.
evidence: The warrior gives strength
the farmer rice
the fisher fish

items.stem: Put these events in story order.
items.why: Step by step he enters the merchant's world.

cards.text: He waits in a rich house

evidence: where he awaited the master of the house
began to read out its contents
Siddhartha wrote and returned the paper
duties of writing important letters and contracts

items.stem: What share of the profits does the friend advise giving Siddhartha?
items.quote: a third of the profits
items.why: The friend proposes a share of both gains and losses.

items.stem: To what does the narrator compare how distant people's lives once seemed?
items.quote: as alien and distant to him as the moon
items.why: Ordinary lives once felt very far from him.

items.stem: Siddhartha plays with his business deals like what?
items.quote: As a ballplayer plays with his balls, he played with his business deals
items.why: Business is like a game to him.

items.stem: Whose bread does Siddhartha say they both eat?
items.quote: they both ate other people’s bread, all people’s bread
items.why: He will not admit he lives off the merchant.

items.stem: Siddhartha lets a street-vendor cheat him out of small change.
items.quote: the street-vendor whom he let cheat him out of some small change
items.why: He doesn't care about small losses.

items.stem: Kamala says Siddhartha is having a merchant's thoughts.
items.quote: again, you’re having a Samana’s thoughts.
items.why: She says a Samana's thoughts.

items.stem: Complete: “But others, a few, are like ____”
items.quote: But others, a few, are like stars
items.why: A few people keep their own course.

items.stem: Match each visitor to what he brings or wants.
items.why: All of these people are welcome to him.
evidence: the merchant who offered him linen for sale
the debtor who sought another loan
the beggar who told him for one hour the story of his poverty

items.stem: What does Siddhartha know little about?
items.quote: Siddhartha knew little about rice and wool, shipping and trade
items.why: He is not trained in trade.

items.stem: Put the rice-trip events in order.
items.why: A failed purchase becomes a pleasant stay.

cards.text: He says he travelled for amusement

evidence: the rice had already been sold to another merchant
Siddhartha stayed for several days in that village
Kamaswami held against him
surely I have travelled for my amusement

items.stem: Why would a man who couldn't fast accept any service?
items.quote: because hunger would force him to do so
items.why: Without fasting, hunger decides for him.

items.stem: Why does the friend suggest sharing profits and losses?
items.quote: Then, he’ll become more zealous.
items.why: The friend hopes a stake will make him eager.

items.stem: Why is Siddhartha never subservient to the merchant?
items.quote: And thinking of Kamala’s words, he was never subservient to the merchant
items.why: Kamala's advice shapes how he acts.

items.stem: Why does Siddhartha keep working, though his soul isn't in trade?
items.quote: The business was good enough to provide him with the money for Kamala
items.why: Business funds his visits.

items.stem: Siddhartha talks easily with people because they interest him.
items.quote: Siddhartha’s interest and curiosity was only concerned with the people
items.why: People, not trade, hold his interest.

items.stem: Siddhartha agrees that inner refuge depends on being smart.
items.quote: “No,” said Siddhartha, “that’s not the reason why.
items.why: He rejects Kamala's explanation.

items.stem: Complete: “for a long time he can allow hunger to ____ him”
items.quote: for a long time he can allow hunger to besiege him
items.why: He can endure hunger without giving in.

items.stem: Complete: “surpassed him, the merchant, in calmness and ____”
items.quote: surpassed him, the merchant, in calmness and equanimity
items.why: His calm makes him useful.

items.stem: Match each cause to its result.
items.why: Each event leads to a response.
evidence: “Excellent,” said Kamaswami.
Kamaswami followed the advice.
a shipment of merchandise seemed to have been lost

items.stem: Order the steps of the interview.
items.why: Siddhartha answers each challenge calmly.

cards.text: He says he is poor by choice
Kamaswami asks if he is destitute
He admits he never planned income

evidence: Might you have become destitute, Brahmin
But I am so voluntarily, and therefore I am not destitute.
have never thought about what I should live off of
a merchant also lives off what other people own

items.stem: “Everyone takes, everyone gives, such is life” mainly turns the talk into what?
items.quote: Everyone takes, everyone gives, such is life.
items.why: He widens the merchant's point to all people.

items.stem: What does the “dying, quiet voice” in his chest suggest?
items.quote: a dying, quiet voice, which admonished him quietly
items.why: His inner voice is growing weak.

items.stem: “or rather they both ate other people's bread” corrects itself to show what?
items.quote: or rather they both ate other people’s bread
items.why: The correction erases the merchant's claim.

items.stem: What does “The source ran somewhere, far away” imply?
items.quote: The source ran somewhere, far away
items.why: The source of his being is not in his life.

items.stem: What distinction does Siddhartha draw in ¶6?
items.quote: But I am so voluntarily, and therefore I am not destitute.
items.why: Choice changes what poverty means.

items.stem: How does “can laugh about it” frame fasting?
items.quote: can allow hunger to besiege him and can laugh about it
items.why: Fasting frees him from need.

items.stem: Calling the beggar “not half as poor as any given Samana” measures poverty by Siddhartha's own past.
items.quote: not half as poor as any given Samana
items.why: He compares with the life he left.

items.stem: “So this one turned out badly!” shows Siddhartha grieving his losses.
items.quote: when he made losses, he laughed and said: “Well, look at this, so this one turned out badly!”
items.why: The line is light, not grieving.

items.stem: Complete: “real life still passing him by and not ____ him”
items.quote: real life still passing him by and not touching him
items.why: Life goes on without reaching him.

items.stem: Order the steps of Siddhartha's argument in ¶42.
items.why: He moves from one man to all people.

Kamaswami is smart but lacks refuge

evidence: Kamaswami is just as smart as I, and still has no refuge in himself.
